children: Bank of America’s Global Research team says the defining contrast of this decade is already visible in two numbers: U.S. nominal GDP has climbed 63% over the past six years, while the price of the U.S. 30-year Treasury yield

That divergence, the team argues, is the market’s scorecard for a 2020s regime of fiscal excess, political populism, de-globalization, resource competition, and trade and AI rivalry. The result has been an inflationary boom that lifted nominal activity even as long-duration government bonds absorbed a historic repricing.

Until higher yields begin to restrain growth, BofA expects investors to remain long equities—particularly while waiting for a possible blow-off in U.S. technology—and short bonds, anticipating a similar climax in yields. The research frames the period as a wholesale inversion of last decade’s playbook: demand-side policy giving way to supply constraints, elite consensus to visible fiscal activism, and open-border globalization to national security screening and border control.

Investment leadership, in this view, is shifting toward AI-related capex, industrial and defense capacity, banks, gold, and assets tied to global rebalancing rather than U.S. exceptionalism or the prior Magnificent Seven concentration. The message is not that the cycle has ended, but that the old regime’s winners are no longer the default. Markets, BofA concludes, will keep riding the boom until yields finally bite.

title: Until yields bite growth, BofA sees a tech climax—and more bond pain
